content: For children, adolescents, pregnant women, and adults experiencing papular pruritic eruptions, antiretroviral therapy (ART) should be considered the primary treatment. Additionally, topical corticosteroids, such as betamethasone valerate, are recommended for managing persistent symptoms. This recommendation is conditional and based on very low-quality evidence. For eosinophilic folliculitis in eligible patients, ART is also the primary treatment. Patients who develop HIV-associated eosinophilic folliculitis after starting ART should not discontinue their ART regimen. If symptoms persist, topical corticosteroids (e.g., betamethasone valerate) can be used. If there is no adequate response, oral itraconazole may be added, and if further treatment is needed, 5% permethrin cream applied above the waist can be considered. This recommendation is conditional and supported by very low-quality evidence. For tinea infections in children and adults, including pregnant women, topical treatments such as terbinafine 1% cream/gel (for two weeks) or miconazole (for three to four weeks) are recommended for non-extensive infections. If there is no response, oral terbinafine or itraconazole should be used. Additionally, individuals with tinea infections and unknown HIV status should be offered an HIV test. These recommendations are conditional and based on very low-quality evidence, except for the HIV testing recommendation, which is strong but supported by low-quality evidence. For herpes zoster in HIV-infected children, adolescents, and adults, including pregnant women, acyclovir is recommended to prevent disease dissemination and promote resolution at any stage of the disease. Individuals presenting with herpes zoster and unknown HIV status should be offered an HIV test and assessed for ART eligibility if the test is positive. These are strong recommendations based on low-quality evidence. For mild to moderate scabies in HIV-infected individuals, including pregnant women, topical permethrin 5% (applied twice) is recommended. If permethrin is unavailable, benzyl benzoate (at least two applications) can be used. If there is poor response or permethrin is not feasible, oral ivermectin at 200 µg/kg is recommended. For severe or crusted scabies in HIV-infected individuals weighing ≥15 kg, two doses of oral ivermectin (spaced one to two weeks apart) are recommended. If ivermectin is unavailable, topical permethrin 5% or benzyl benzoate should be used until the condition is clinically clear, as longer treatments may be required. For children weighing <15 kg with severe scabies, topical permethrin 5% or benzyl benzoate should be used until clinically clear. Additionally, keratolytics like 5% salicylic acid can be used to remove scale bulk. These recommendations are conditional and based on very low-quality evidence. For extensive or unusually distributed molluscum contagiosum in HIV-infected patients, ART should be considered the primary treatment. No additional specific treatment is recommended. Adults presenting with new-onset molluscum contagiosum in high HIV-prevalence settings and unknown HIV status should be offered an HIV test and assessed for ART eligibility if positive. These recommendations are conditional and based on very low-quality evidence, except for the HIV testing recommendation, which is strong but supported by low-quality evidence. For oropharyngeal candidiasis in adults, oral fluconazole (100–150 mg daily for 7–14 days) is the preferred treatment. If fluconazole is unavailable or contraindicated, alternatives include topical therapy with nystatin suspension or pastilles, or clotrimazole troches. For children, oral fluconazole (3 mg/kg daily for 7–14 days) is the preferred treatment. In cases of mild oropharyngeal candidiasis in children, topical therapy with nystatin suspension or pastilles (or clotrimazole troches) is recommended. Prompt ART initiation is strongly recommended for all HIV-infected individuals with oropharyngeal candidiasis. These recommendations are strong, with evidence quality ranging from moderate to high. For Stevens-Johnson syndrome (SJS) and toxic epidermal necrolysis (TEN) in HIV-infected individuals, the suspected causative drug should be promptly discontinued, and supportive therapies should be provided. The use of systemic corticosteroids is not recommended. These recommendations are strong but based on very low-quality evidence. Skin and oral conditions are common in HIV-infected individuals, particularly in resource-limited settings, affecting up to 90% of patients during their illness. These conditions can cause significant morbidity and mortality, especially when associated with advanced immunosuppression. Early recognition and management of these conditions, along with prompt initiation of ART, are critical to improving patient outcomes and quality of life.
